results.note: McCann p.132 Results 5-HIAA 1st para and Table 4 p.133: 15.2 (7.9; range 4.8-37.3) vs 10.3 (3.1), F(1,54)=11.6 p=.001, group F(1,52)=14.9 p<.001. Recomputed the editors' figures: 4.9/15.2 = 32% lower; Welch 95% CI 1.7 to 8.1. All match.

McCann p.132 text gives 46% vs 20% and the control male/female difference; Table 4 p.133 marks MDMA female vs control female (section symbol) and leaves MDMA male unmarked; subgroup means and n (10.1/18.7, 12 v 11; 10.8/13.4, 18 v 17) as stated.
McCann p.132, 3rd paragraph of the 5-HIAA subsection: r = -0.2, p = .33 for number of exposures; duration, frequency and time since last use stated as not significant with no coefficients.
McCann Table 3, p.131: every count and percentage matches, including cannabis 28 (93%) vs 22 printed as 73%.
McCann p.135, Discussion 1st paragraph: contains both the matched-for-education-and-other-drug-use sentence and the CSF-data-alone caveat, and the monkey-decrement reasoning.
McCann p.133, Prolactin 1st-2nd paragraphs and Table 5: gender effects on basal, peak change and AUC; no significant drug effects.
Ung Table 3 p.280 and Results Learning and memory 2nd para p.279: -1.37 (-2.65, -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02; -1.06 (-1.98, -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58.
Ung Patterns of MDMA use paragraph: begins p.276, the sentences cited are on p.279 col.1; two alcohol/tobacco control studies (Morgan 1999; Morgan et al. 2002), one drug-naive (Taurah et al. 2014).
Ung p.279 Critical appraisal 1st paragraph: all 3 cohorts poor, 5 of 11 case-control fair and 6 poor, comparability and matching concerns, self-report exposure in 12 of 14.
Murphy p.172, Discussion 1st paragraph: wording of the four conclusions matches.
Murphy p.161, updating 1st paragraph: 9 studies, all but one by combinations of the authors, 7 computation span deficits, 2.48 span items (2.75 vs 5.23), 27 of 44 shared.

Murphy Discussion 3rd paragraph, begins p.172 and continues p.173: only reference [47] (Schilt et al. 2007) prospective; cross-sectional or quasi-experimental otherwise; the slow-prospective and unethical-experiment arguments are both there.
Halpern PMC Results 1st paragraph: about 1500 screened, about 250 to baseline, 116 completed, 5 excluded on hair or urine, 111 evaluable (52 and 59), criteria relaxed for 6.

Halpern Table 2: CVLT 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, -0.5 (-4.2, 3.2), p=0.79; logical memory 0.7 (-3.6, 5.0) and 0.7 (-2.4, 3.8); verbal paired associates delayed 0.1 (-0.7, 0.8); Rey-Osterrieth delayed 0.8 (-1.8, 3.4). Differences are non-users minus users, as the table's footnote says.

Halpern Table 2: vocabulary 4.7 (1.1, 8.4) p=0.01; digit symbol 7.1 (1.0, 13.2) p=0.02; spatial span forward 0.8 (0.0, 1.6) p=0.04; non-dominant pegboard -5.0 (-9.3, -0.7) p=0.02; Raven's p=0.05 and digits backwards p=0.05; verbal IQ 6.0 (-0.2, 12.2) p=0.06.

Halpern Table 3 heavy column (n=22): RSAT brief items 79.5 vs 88.5, 8.7 (3.1, 14.4) p=0.003; pegboard -8.4 (-13.9, -2.8) p=0.003; vocabulary 5.0 (0.2, 9.8) p=0.04; no other p<0.05 in that column (nearest are spatial span total and backward, p=0.09). The verbal-IQ and BDI re-adjustment is stated in Results 2nd paragraph.

Halpern Results 2nd paragraph and Figure 1 legend: coefficient -1.4 (-2.3, -0.4), p=0.004, log-transformed episodes, adjusted for age, gender and race/ethnicity; Pearson r = -0.37; scatter plot inspected for outliers.

Halpern Results 3rd paragraph and Table 4: the 14 values run 0.37 (WCST perseverations) to 0.76 (spatial span total), and the text says many for the medium effect. Table 4's column is the effect that can be REJECTED at p<0.05, so 'the largest effect not excluded' is a boundary paraphrase. Counting values at or below 0.50, a medium effect is excluded on 6 of 14 (5 if the threshold is read strictly below 0.5); a large effect is excluded on all 14.

Halpern Discussion 1st-2nd paragraphs: vocabulary read as premorbid because vocabulary survives neurological insult; lighter-use-only differences and the pegboard difference called chance; RSAT the only consistent finding, read as reflection impulsivity that cross-sectional data cannot show to be caused by ecstasy.
Halpern Table 1: father 53.9 vs 27.1 p=0.006; mother 61.5 vs 27.1 p<0.001; white 76.9 vs 91.5 p=0.04; raves median 98 vs 45 p=0.005; marijuana intoxications median 10 vs 1 p<0.001.

Schilt p.731, Neuropsychological Testing 1st paragraph: multivariate (Pillai) F(12,96)=0.73, p=.72, partial eta squared 0.08, in the 58 and 60 analysed. The baseline comparison is one multivariate test, not 12 separate tests.
Schilt Table 2 p.732 RAVLT immediate row and text p.731: 58.7 to 59.6 vs 57.8 to 61.7, changes 0.86 (5.5) and 3.90 (5.8), B 2.23 (0.17 to 4.29), F(1,108)=4.62, p=.03.
Schilt Table 2 delayed recall row and text: 13.8 to 13.2 vs 13.5 to 14.1, changes -0.52 (1.8) and 0.65 (1.8), B 0.63 (0.05 to 1.22), F(1,108)=4.67, p=.03.

Schilt Table 2 recognition row, its footnote and text p.732: 29.95 to 29.66 vs 29.88 to 29.93; 22.4% vs 6.7% declined; text gives odds ratio 5.87, Wald chi-square 5.62, p=.02 (footnote rounds to 5.9). The anchor does not use Table 2's printed B of 1.77, which is the logarithm of that odds ratio.
Schilt Table 2: the nine other rows run p=.21 (JOLO) to .85 (PASAT 2.4 s); text p.732 states no sex x ecstasy interaction on RAVLT scores.
Schilt p.732, 3rd paragraph: F(1,92)=6.62, p=.01, partial eta squared 0.07, with 43 and 57 people; covariance effect of cocaine and d-amphetamine but not alcohol, tobacco or cannabis.

Schilt Table 1 and text p.731: 3.2 (5.2) tablets, median 1.5, range 0.5-30, mean period 1.6 months; last use 11.8 (12.0) weeks, median 7.9; intervals 11.1 (6.2) vs 19.1 (7.5) months, t(116)=6.30, p<.001.

Schilt Table 1 and text p.731: cannabis 48.8 vs 17.2 joints p=.04 at baseline and 53.6 vs 20.5 p<.001 at follow-up; cocaine 1.4 vs 0.3 times p=.006 at follow-up; no baseline differences in smoking, alcohol, d-amphetamines or cocaine.
Schilt p.732, Comment 1st paragraph, last sentence: performance of all participants within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population.

Schilt Comment 2nd paragraph (p.732-733) lists cannabis, cocaine/amphetamine, sensation seeking from the wider cohort, depression and the information given at entry; the 6th paragraph (p.733-734) lists the limitations named, including the retest-interval argument, tablet content and the educated, motivated sample.

Ung Table 3 p.280 and text p.279: overall 0.03 (-0.35, 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77; sensitivity analysis excluding Gouzoulis-Mayfrank et al. (2005), the poor-quality cohort, left it unchanged; subtest values -0.17, -0.01, 0.00, 0.24, all intervals including zero.
Same Table 3 rows as anchor n 7; numbers match.
Ung p.279, last sentence of the Learning and memory 2nd paragraph: the progressive effect of abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested because of the small sample.

Ung p.279, 3rd paragraph: Reneman et al. (2001b) and Ward et al. (2006) impairment despite 12-24 months; Zakzanis and Campbell (2006), 2-year, poor quality, improvement in those who stopped and deterioration in those who continued.

Ung Executive function 1st paragraph, p.279-280: 10 studies; two poor-quality prospective studies neither improved nor deteriorated at 18 months; seven case-control studies no significant difference; four by the same primary author with the same abstinent participants showed the between-groups trend.
Same text as anchor n 10, p.279 Critical appraisal; numbers match.
Same text as anchor n 9; matches.

Ung p.279 Duration of abstinence: 8, 1, 2, 2, 1 studies at 6, 12, 18, 24 and 48 months (14 in all); Discussion 6th paragraph p.281-282 gives Taurah et al. (2014) as lowest exposure (36-69 tablets) with the longest abstinence and states no formal dose-response analysis was conducted.

Ung abstract p.273 ('based on low-quality findings'), Discussion 8th paragraph (trait impulsivity, may always have performed differently) and 9th paragraph (do not definitively confirm permanent damage nor that it is due to neurotoxic effects), Conclusion p.282 ('variable, low-quality findings').

Ung p.281, Discussion 5th paragraph: Muller et al. (2019), 16 neuroimaging studies, lower SERT in 8 of 13 regions, meta-regression positive association with time abstinent, noted as largely driven by one small study - which the paper names as Selvaraj et al. (2009), not Muller; Thomasius et al. (2006), 2.5 years abstinent, potential SERT recovery with no improvement in verbal memory.
